newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Solana silent after five hours of talks in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Solana silent after five hours of talks in Russia.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana had five hours of talks on Monday with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on the alliance's enlargement plans, but left the country without making any comment.
In a sign of the sensitivity of the talks, Solana met Primakov at a secret venue outside Moscow and did not speak to reporters once during 24 hours in Russia.

Primakov was also tight-lipped, but Interfax news agency quoted foreign ministry sources as saying he had summoned other officials to a special meeting to discuss the results of the talks. It gave no details.

NATO said Solana was seeking to reassure Moscow about the alliance's plans to admit new members from eastern and central Europe. The Kremlin said the meeting was only the first step towards working out a new relationship.
"It is just the first round...in mutual relations between Russia and NATO," Sergei Yastrzhembsky, President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary, told a Kremlin briefing.
"I wouldn't have raised expectations about this meeting between Solana and Primakov," he said.
Interfax quoted foreign ministry sources as saying a statement on the talks might be released later on Monday.
Solana has been expected to offer some form of permanent consultative forum between the former Cold War foes, greater flexibility on arms control issues and more economic assistance.
But both sides played down chances of a breakthrough in the long dispute, particularly in the absence of Yeltsin, who has been in hospital with pneumonia.
Little time remains for reaching an understanding before a July summit in Madrid at which NATO is expected to issue invitations to the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland.
Both sides would welcome an agreement before that but reaching it will be difficult.

"Solana faces a hard task -- to convince his eastern neighbour that taking former socialist countries into NATO does not threaten its security and strengthens stability in Europe," Russia's NTV commercial television said.

"The Russian leader's absence from the Kremlin disturbs Western representatives. In their opinion, neither Primakov... nor anyone else can independently take decisions determining what Russia and all Europe will be like in the next century."

NATO's proposed expansion is again on Moscow's agenda after a year in which attention focused first on presidential elections, which Yeltsin won, in July and then on his heart problems, which kept him out of the Kremlin until December 23.

Russia launched a new diplomatic offensive against the alliance's plans after Yeltsin returned briefly to the Kremlin and ordered the foreign ministry to start drawing up a set of possible responses to an enlarged NATO.

Diplomats say Russia appears intent on delaying enlargement, limiting the number of countries that join NATO and seeking as many concessions as possible over one of the few issues which unites Russian politicians across the political spectrum.
It was far from certain that NATO's proposals for forging a special relationship would meet Russia's demands, which include a say in all issues covering its "vital interests".
